rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says each human body develops from organic and inorganic substances also found in the earth, elaborating the successive stages in 71:14.
rows.anchor: the evolution of the individual human body out of the same substances - both organic and inorganic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase also refers to human species evolution from primitive organisms through increasingly complex bodily, mental, and spiritual development.
rows.anchor: the evolution of the human species, which, starting from the most primitive organisms living on earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the phrase as a final bringing-forth.
rows.anchor: Lit., "with a [final] bringing-forth ".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following Jawhari, Baydawi, Lisan al-'Arab, and Qamus, Asad defines tartil as distinct, orderly, unhurried arrangement; in recitation it is calm, measured delivery that considers the meaning.
rows.anchor: The term tartil primarily denotes "the putting [of something] together distinctly, in a well-arranged manner, and without any haste"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant of the phrase in 25:32 has a somewhat different sense, describing the manner in which the Qur'an was revealed.
rows.anchor: A somewhat different significance attaches to a variant of this phrase in 25:32, applying to the manner in which the Qur'an was revealed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's literal gloss is those who are with the Prophet.
rows.anchor: Lit., "of those who are with thee".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing passage returns to the opening verses' theme of the spiritual value of night prayer.
rows.anchor: With this concluding passage, the discourse returns to the theme of the opening verses, namely, the great spiritual value of praying at night.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about not counting it refers to measuring the length of the night vigil.
rows.anchor: Lit., "count it", i.e., the length of your vigil.

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators infer that all of verse 20 was revealed at Medina because fighting in God's cause was sanctioned only after the Hijrah.
rows.anchor: This reference to "fighting in God's cause" has induced many commentators to assume that the whole of verse 20 was revealed at Medina

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathir
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads the future-tense wording as a prediction of later circumstances, the interpretation Asad adopts against the Medinan dating.
rows.anchor: as Ibn Kathir points out, be understood as a prediction of future circumstances.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects the dating inference as unwarranted: the future tense predicts later circumstances, although jihad was first sanctioned in Medina.
rows.anchor: the sentence in question is clearly expressed in the future tense: "in time there will be" (sayakun) - and must, therefore, as Ibn Kathir points out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage emphasizes avoiding exaggeration even in devotional practice.
rows.anchor: the above passage stresses the necessity of avoiding all exaggeration even in one's devotions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad identifies this as the Qur'an's earliest instance of zakah and refers readers to his note 34 on surah 2 for an explanation.
rows.anchor: For an explanation of the term zakah - of which the above is the earliest Qur'anic instance - see surah 2, note 34.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qutila literally means he has been killed, or as an imprecation, may he be killed; Asad says a literal rendering is meaningless here.
rows.anchor: The expression qutila reads, literally, "he has been killed" or, as an imprecation, "may he be killed".

rows.speaker: many commentators (Tabari among them)
rows.claim: Many commentators, including Tabari, understand the expression as rejection from God's grace, a spiritual killing.
rows.anchor: many commentators (Tabari among them) understand it as signifying "he is rejected from God's grace" (lu'ina)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders it as self-destruction caused by the man's own action or attitude.
rows.anchor: killed" spiritually by his own action or attitude; hence my rendering, "he destroys himself".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to 96:6-7 for comparison.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sihr usually means sorcery or magic; its primary sense is changing something from its proper or natural state, as Taj al-'Arus explains.
rows.anchor: the turning of something from its proper [or "natural"] state of being into another state

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sihr can describe the fascination or enchantment produced by exceptional, spellbinding eloquence.
rows.anchor: often applied to the fascination or enchantment caused by exceptional, "spellbinding" eloquence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When deniers use sihr for a divine message, it also implies deliberate deception or delusion.
rows.anchor: used by deniers of the truth to describe a divine message - it has also the connotation of wilful deception

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's question points to the many people who refuse to listen to the truth.
rows.anchor: I.e., with so many people who refuse to listen to the truth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the demand as scriptures opened wide, or unfolded so that everyone could understand them.
rows.anchor: Lit., "everyone of them wants to be given wide-open scriptures", or "scriptures unfolded" (i.e., open to everyone's understanding)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad compares this demand with 2:118, where people ask for a direct message from God without a prophet's intervention.
rows.anchor: 2:118 - "Why does not God speak unto us, nor is a message conveyed to us?"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad calls this the Qur'an's earliest illustration of the arrogance or false pride it frequently condemns.
rows.anchor: The above is the earliest illustration of the "arrogance" or "false pride" to which the Qur'an so often refers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To be left without purpose means not being held morally responsible for one's actions.
rows.anchor: I.e., without being held morally responsible for his doings.

none: translation followed by broken, contextless fragments of notes

words: إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكَ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ تَنزِيلًۭا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal form nazzalna implies that Qur'anic revelation came gradually.
rows.anchor: The gradualness of Qur'anic revelation is implied in the verbal form nazzalna.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The great sign is God's guidance, offered through measureless grace even to the most recalcitrant sinner.
rows.anchor: "showed him the great wonder", i.e., of the guidance which God, in His measureless grace, offers even to the most recalcitrant sinner.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here, heaven is a metonym for the cosmic system, as elsewhere in the Qur'an; Asad points to his note on 2:29.
rows.anchor: The "heaven" is here, as in many other places in the Qur'an, a metonym for "cosmic system"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage echoes 40:56-57; Asad says both passages counter a man-centered universe by stressing humanity's smallness beside cosmic vastness and complexity.
rows.anchor: Both these passages refute the "man-centred" view of the universe by pointing out man's insignificance as compared with the vastness and complexity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says 87:2 is the earliest instance in revelation chronology of sawwa used in this sense.
rows.anchor: the earliest instance, in the chronology of Qur'anic revelation, of the use of the verb sawwa in the above sense.

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi explains pasture metonymically as all herbal produce suitable for human or animal consumption.
rows.anchor: The term "pasture" (mar'a) connotes here, metonymically, all herbal produce suitable for consumption by man or animal (Razi).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The provision for people and animals implies gratitude to God and awareness that He is the Provider, as in the food passage 80:24-32.
rows.anchor: Implying (as in 80:24-32) that man ought to be grateful to God, and should always be conscious of His being the Provider

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This gratitude theme leads into the discourse's return to resurrection and ultimate judgment.
rows.anchor: hence the subsequent return of the discourse to the theme of resurrection and ultimate judgment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's literal gloss says it is not upon the Prophet if the man does not attain purity.
rows.anchor: Lit., "it is not upon thee (alayka) that he does not attain to purity".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means that God makes man's way easy.
rows.anchor: Lit., "He makes easy the way for him".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It alludes to man's intellectual equipment for distinguishing good from evil and making fruitful use of opportunities in his earthly environment.
rows.anchor: enabling him to discern between good and evil and to make fruitful use of the opportunities offered to him by his earthly environment.
